title: Galilee Ministry Landscapes
subtitle: Nazareth, Capernaum, the lake, and disputed shoreline geography
summary: Move among Lower Galilee, the northwestern lakeshore, Sea of Galilee crossings, and the northeastern shore while keeping established places, candidate sites, and unknown event locations distinct.
disclaimer: The current panorama is a project-authored schematic landscape, not a photograph of first-century Galilee. Established sites such as Nazareth, Capernaum, Magdala, and the Sea of Galilee are distinguished from disputed Cana/Bethsaida identifications, traditional sermon locations, and unknown boat-event positions.

evidenceLegend.label: Schematic landscape
evidenceLegend.description: The visible hills, shoreline, water, and vegetation are generic teaching geometry until verified period-appropriate visual assets are supplied.

evidenceLegend.label: Archaeological anchor
evidenceLegend.description: An established excavated settlement or securely identified place represented by an existing atlas record.

evidenceLegend.label: Traditional location
evidenceLegend.description: A later commemorative location that is historically meaningful but not established by the Gospel text.

evidenceLegend.label: Unknown / disputed geography
evidenceLegend.description: A Gospel place or event whose exact modern coordinate is unresolved and must not be forced into one pin.

evidenceLegend.label: Travel / regional interpretation
evidenceLegend.description: A broad geographic relationship or reconstructed movement corridor rather than an exact witnessed route.

panorama.alt: A schematic interactive Galilee landscape used to compare Lower Galilee, lakeshore settlements, lake crossings, and disputed shoreline geography; not a photographic reconstruction.

comparison.label: Galilee ministry settings
comparison.intro: Switch among broad ministry settings. The views teach geographic relationships; they do not assert a continuous day-by-day route for Jesus.

options.label: Lower Galilee
options.summary: Nazareth is securely identified within Lower Galilee, while Cana remains disputed and intentionally unpinned.
options.rationale: The Gospel narratives locate important early ministry traditions in this broader Lower Galilee setting.
options.objections: The exact route between Nazareth, Cana, and other villages is not preserved, and Cana cannot responsibly be reduced to one candidate.

options.label: NW lakeshore
options.summary: Capernaum and Magdala provide strong archaeological anchors for the inhabited western and northwestern lakeshore.
options.rationale: Both settlements help users understand first-century village life and the lake economy without identifying individual Gospel houses.
options.objections: The schematic shoreline and settlement silhouettes are not archaeological plans and do not reproduce first-century building footprints.

options.label: Lake crossings
options.summary: The Sea of Galilee is certain geography; the exact tracks of individual Gospel boat crossings are not recoverable.
options.rationale: The existing journey system can show narrative sequences while preserving route certainty separately from the physical lake.
options.objections: Wind, landing point, boat track, and event position on the water are not known precisely enough for a historical GPS route.

options.label: Bethsaida question
options.summary: Bethsaida is textually important but archaeologically debated; el-Araj and et-Tell remain separate candidates.
options.rationale: Showing the candidates side by side communicates the live geographic debate better than assigning the Gospel place one normal pin.
options.objections: Ancient shoreline reconstruction is part of the debate and requires verified geomorphological evidence before a period shoreline is drawn.

hotspots.label: Nazareth
hotspots.summary: Established early Roman settlement and Gospel hometown setting.

whyShown.evidence: Ancient Nazareth is securely identified and archaeology supports early Roman settlement.
whyShown.inference: The drawn village is not a reconstruction of a specific excavated quarter.
whyShown.alternatives: Individual Gospel houses or the exact synagogue episode location are not recoverable.

hotspots.label: Cana remains unresolved
hotspots.summary: The Gospel village is represented conceptually rather than as a single modern coordinate.

whyShown.evidence: John names Cana of Galilee, but the existing atlas record intentionally has no normal pin.
whyShown.inference: This hotspot is an explanatory position within a schematic landscape, not a geographic coordinate for Cana.
whyShown.alternatives: Khirbet Qana and Kafr Kanna remain distinct candidate/traditional identifications.

hotspots.label: Capernaum
hotspots.summary: Securely identified village central to many Gospel ministry narratives.

whyShown.evidence: Kfar Nahum securely identifies ancient Capernaum and preserves Roman-period settlement remains.
whyShown.inference: The foreground structures are schematic and not a plan of excavated Capernaum.
whyShown.alternatives: Specific houses associated with named Gospel figures remain interpretive.

hotspots.label: Magdala
hotspots.summary: Excavated early Roman lakeside settlement with first-century synagogue context.

whyShown.evidence: The ancient settlement is securely located and excavated.
whyShown.inference: No particular Gospel visit by Jesus is invented here.
whyShown.alternatives: The relationship among the ancient names Magdala, Migdal, and Tarichaeae requires nuance.

hotspots.label: Sermon mountain — traditional area
hotspots.summary: The modern Mount of Beatitudes is a later commemorative location, not a proven sermon coordinate.

whyShown.evidence: Matthew refers to a mountain but does not identify it by name.
whyShown.inference: The traditional area is useful for orientation only.
whyShown.alternatives: The actual sermon location remains unknown.

hotspots.label: Sea of Galilee
hotspots.summary: Certain physical lake; individual Gospel crossing tracks are generally unrecoverable.

whyShown.evidence: The lake itself is geographically certain and central to Gospel narratives.
whyShown.inference: The displayed water surface is a schematic visual, and no route line on it is historical measurement.
whyShown.alternatives: Journey animation should continue to label generalized or reconstructed crossings as such.

hotspots.label: The “other side”
hotspots.summary: Gerasenes, Gadarenes, and Gergesenes textual/geographic forms should not collapse into one landing point.

whyShown.evidence: The textual tradition preserves multiple place-name forms east of the lake.
whyShown.inference: This explanatory hotspot does not identify the landing site.
whyShown.alternatives: Gadara/Kursi and other discussions should remain contextual or candidate-level.

hotspots.label: Bethsaida — competing candidates
hotspots.summary: The Gospel place remains unpinned while el-Araj and et-Tell are maintained as separate candidates.

whyShown.evidence: The Gospel place is clear textually but its archaeological identification remains debated.
whyShown.inference: The hotspot is conceptual and does not replace either candidate record.
whyShown.alternatives: el-Araj and et-Tell remain independently selectable archaeological candidates.

mapCamera.note: Regional 3D teaching camera over the Sea of Galilee basin. Candidate Bethsaida volumes remain explicitly disputed.

siteModel.label: Galilee site-volume layer
siteModel.note: Project-authored display geometry for identified and candidate site zones. It does not reconstruct first-century buildings or a precise c. 30 CE shoreline.

provenance.notes: Site-scale display volumes only; Bethsaida alternatives remain candidate-site geometry.

reconstruction.title: Sea of Galilee c. 30 CE — animated reconstruction
reconstruction.alt: Layered artistic reconstruction of the Sea of Galilee with basalt shore settlements, boats, reeds, and surrounding hills.
reconstruction.note: Animated artistic reconstruction. The lake basin and established settlements provide geographic anchors; exact shoreline, boats, vegetation density, and village appearance are illustrative.
